newsitem.title: MALI: Mali reruns elections but opposition boycotts.
newsitem.headline: Mali reruns elections but opposition boycotts.

text.p: Mali, one of the stars of Africa's 1990s democracy movement, holds a rerun of a chaotic April parliamentary election on Sunday with the main opposition boycotting the poll.

One day after war-racked Liberia turned out in force to vote in elections to end seven years of civil war, impoverished Mali wraps up its troubled second multi-party national elections with part of the electorate likely to stay away.
Adding to the uncertainty, the 18 opposition parties refusing to take part have called nationwide marches as part of a campaign for the whole process to be scrapped and reorganised.

An estimated 3,000 opposition activists marched through the capital Bamako on Saturday on the eve of polling. Police and paramilitary gendarmes, who will ensure public order during polling and not the army, did not intervene.
After the march, witnesses said some opposition militants set fire to tyres.
Almost 600 candidates from President Alpha Oumar Konare's Alliance for Democracy in Mali (ADEMA), 18 other parties and 13 independent lists will contest the 147 national assembly seats.
Polling starts at 8 a.m. (0800 GMT) and ends at 6 p.m. Some five million Malians are eligible to vote.
Konare's government has not formally banned protests but informed sources say that mixed patrols of police and gendarmes will take strict measures to ensure security during polling.

The arid, land-locked, mainly-Moslem former French colony is named after a pre-colonial African empire that built its power on gold and flourished when Europe was in the Middle Ages. Gold remains a major source of foreign exchange.

Mali was widely praised for its 1992 transition from Moussa Traore's dictatorship to a multiparty system. Widely respected military leader Amadou Toumani Toure steered the country to elections and then, unlike most coup leaders, stepped down.

An independent electoral commission is running the elections. The constitutional court scrapped the April 13 parliamentary poll, citing organisational chaos. The commission said it had lacked time to prepare properly.

The opposition wanted the whole election timetable revised but Konare, a historian elected in 1992, pressed ahead with only minor modifications and won a May 11 presidential election -- also boycotted by the main opposition.
The opposition alliance includes some politicians associated with Moussa Traore.
Religious leaders have called for peaceful polling after failing to bring the two sides any closer after 27 meetings.

First results are expected on Sunday night. Final results, which must be ratified by the constitutional court, are likely within 72 hours, election officials say. A second round is planned for August 3.
The turnout on April 13 was around 30 percent.
